panels.introHtml:
Start here

PrivateBin, the zero-knowledge pastebin

A map of PrivateBin/PrivateBin 2.1.1 in C4 terms: context on the overview, the client, server and storage on the full map.

PrivateBin was originally written by Sébastien Sauvage (© 2012) and is developed by the PrivateBin contributors under the zlib/libpng licence. This map describes it in its own words and is not affiliated with its authors.

Try it

  • Open a card to see its part of the system.
  • Play Create a paste to see where the encryption happens.
  • Click a component for what it does and where it lives in the code.
panels.overviewHtml:
The full map

The browser does the work

PrivateBin runs as PHP on any web server; the client is one JavaScript file. Both are opened up into their components.

How to read it

People on the left, the browser client and the PHP server in the middle, storage on the right. Only one storage backend is active in an install.

people.title: People
people.text: Two roles, both anonymous: the author who creates a paste and anyone the link is shared with.

browser.title: Encrypt in the browser
browser.text: The JavaScript client does the real work: it encrypts before sending and decrypts after fetching.

server.title: Accept, never read
server.line2: JSON in, JSON or a page out.
server.text: A small PHP app that routes requests, limits abuse and serves the page. It never sees a key.

rules.title: Expire and burn
rules.text: The server enforces the only rules it can: how long a paste lives and who may delete it.

storage.title: Keep only ciphertext
storage.text: Pluggable storage behind one interface; whatever the backend, it holds encrypted blobs.

outside.title: Outside services
outside.text: The only outside system PrivateBin talks to, and only if configured.

nodes.what: Writes a paste, picks how long it lives, and gets back a link to share.
nodes.why: The author is the only one who ever sees the key being made: it is created in their browser and goes into the link.

nodes.what: Opens a shared link, reads the paste and, if the discussion is open, comments on it.
nodes.why: Whoever holds the full link can read the paste. Without the part after # the server's copy is noise.

nodes.what: A YOURLS, Shlink or Chhoto instance that turns the long paste link into a short one.
nodes.why: Paste links are long because they carry the key. A shortener makes them easy to share, at the price of handing the full link, key included, to that service.
nodes.tools: YOURLS, Shlink or Chhoto API, set in cfg/conf.php

nodes.what: The single page: editor, paste viewer, attachments and the discussion. It reads the key from the link and drives every step.
nodes.why: All the product logic runs here, so the server can stay a dumb, blind store.

nodes.what: Makes a random 256-bit key, compresses the text with zlib and encrypts it with AES-256-GCM; a password, if set, is mixed in with PBKDF2.
nodes.why: This is the zero-knowledge promise: the server only ever receives ciphertext, so a breach or a subpoena yields nothing readable.
nodes.tools: js/privatebin.js CryptTool · WebCrypto API · zlib in WebAssembly

nodes.what: Sends and fetches JSON: the encrypted paste, comments, deletions and shortener requests.
nodes.why: One small layer decides what crosses the network, which makes it easy to check that the key never does.

nodes.what: Every request lands in index.php; the controller picks create, read, delete, a shortener call or the page, and answers with JSON or HTML.
nodes.why: One entry point and no router: the operation is read from the method and the query string, which keeps the PHP side tiny.

nodes.what: Renders the one HTML page with the settings the client needs: expiry options, formats, feature switches and a strict CSP.
nodes.why: The page carries no paste data. It is the same for every paste; the client fetches the paste afterwards.

nodes.what: Lets one IP create one paste every 10 seconds by default, or only listed IP ranges at all.
nodes.why: A public pastebin is an easy spam target. The IP is stored only as a keyed hash, so the limit works without keeping addresses.

nodes.what: Checks the settings that travel in clear text, turns the expiry choice into a date, makes the ID and the delete token, and deletes a paste when it has expired or was read once.
nodes.why: Expiry and burn-after-reading are enforced here, on the server, because the server is the only party that can actually delete the data.

nodes.what: Deletes up to 10 expired pastes, at most once every 5 minutes, while handling a new paste.
nodes.why: There is no cron job to set up. Expired pastes nobody opens again would otherwise stay on disk forever.

nodes.what: One interface for pastes, comments and small values (server salt, limiter times); the config picks the backend.
nodes.why: Hosting differs a lot between installs, so storage is a plug-in: a folder by default, a database or a bucket when you need one.
nodes.tools: lib/Data/AbstractData.php and one class per backend · [model] in the config

nodes.what: Calls the configured URL shortener from the server and shows the short link.
nodes.why: The shortener's API key stays on the server instead of being shipped to every browser.

nodes.what: One file per paste under data/ab/cd/, comments in a folder beside it.
nodes.why: Works on any PHP host with no database at all, which is why it is the default.

nodes.what: Three tables: pastes, comments and a small key-value config table.
nodes.why: For installs that already run a database or need several web servers to share the data.

nodes.what: Each paste as one object in a bucket.
nodes.why: For serverless or container hosting where the local disk does not last.

zones.label: Storage · one backend, set in config

create.title: Create a paste
create.desc: An author writes a paste. The browser encrypts it, the server stores a blob it cannot read, and the key ends up only in the link.

hops.t: The author types the text, adds files if they like, picks an expiry, burn after reading or an open discussion, and maybe a password.

A fresh random 256-bit key. The text is compressed with zlib and encrypted with AES-256-GCM; the key is stretched with PBKDF2 (100,000 rounds), mixed with the password if there is one. The settings ride along as authenticated data, so the server cannot change them unnoticed.
The request body is {v: 2, ct, adata, meta: {expire}}: ciphertext and the few settings the server must act on. No key, no plaintext.
A POST, so Request sets the operation to create. The controller checks the size limit (10 MB) and the envelope's format.
The traffic limiter hashes the IP with the server salt and refuses a second paste from it within 10 seconds.
The last post time per IP hash is a small value in the same store as the pastes.
Paste rules turn the expiry choice into a date, reject a discussion on a burn-after-reading paste, and name the paste by a 64-bit hash of the ciphertext. Each paste gets its own salt.
The storage adapter writes the paste through the configured backend.
With the default backend, one JSON file: data/ab/cd/abcd….php, prefixed so the web server never serves it.
The answer: the paste ID and a delete token, an HMAC of the ID with that paste's salt.
The browser builds ?id#key with the key in base58 after the #. Browsers never send the fragment to a server, so the key stays with whoever has the link.

read.title: Open a paste
read.desc: A reader opens the link. The page arrives first, then the ciphertext, and the browser decrypts it with the key from the fragment.

hops.t: The reader opens https://host/?id#key. The browser requests /?id only; the key stays in the address bar.
The server answers with the same page as for any paste: template, scripts and settings, no paste data.
The client reads the ID from the query string and asks for the paste as JSON.
A GET with a paste ID and a JSON Accept header: the read operation.
If the paste has expired it is deleted now and the reader gets the same error as for a paste that never existed. A burn-after-reading paste is deleted as it is handed out.
The stored blob, its comments and the remaining lifetime are loaded. The paste's salt is removed from the answer.
Ciphertext, authenticated settings and the encrypted comments come back.
The key from the fragment, decoded from base58, decrypts the paste. If that fails, the reader is asked for the password and it is tried again.
The plaintext is shown with the chosen format: plain text, syntax highlighting or Markdown, cleaned with DOMPurify.

purge.title: Clean up expired pastes
purge.desc: There is no scheduler. Expired pastes are removed while new ones are created, and any expired paste is removed the moment someone asks for it.

hops.t: A new paste arrives. Cleanup piggybacks on this request, so a busy instance cleans up often and a quiet one rarely.
The purge limiter allows one round every 5 minutes, remembered as a small value in the store.
The backend lists up to 10 expired pastes and deletes them with their comments.
On disk that means unlinking the paste file and its discussion folder.

shorten.title: Shorten the link
shorten.desc: The long link with its key is sent to an outside shortener through the server, which holds the API key.

hops.t: After creating a paste, the author clicks Shorten (or it happens on its own when configured). The client opens ?shortenviayourls&link=… with the full link.
The controller sees a shortener operation and builds the proxy for the configured service.
The proxy checks that the link points to this instance, so it cannot be used to shorten arbitrary URLs.
It calls the shortener's API with the server-side key.
hops.note: The shortener receives the full link, key included. Anyone running it can read the paste.

hops.t: The short link is shown on a small page of its own.

buildSteps.title: A pastebin
buildSteps.text: Store text under an ID and give it back: a page, a JSON API and files on disk.
buildSteps.decision: No framework and no router: index.php builds one controller that reads the operation from the request.

buildSteps.title: Zero knowledge
buildSteps.text: Encrypt in the browser and put the key in the URL fragment.
buildSteps.decision: The key lives after #, which browsers never send, so the server stores ciphertext it cannot decrypt.

buildSteps.title: Pastes that disappear
buildSteps.text: Expiry dates, burn after reading and cleanup without a cron job.
buildSteps.decision: Purging rides on new pastes, rate-limited to once every 5 minutes, so there is nothing extra to deploy.

buildSteps.title: Abuse limits
buildSteps.text: One paste per IP every few seconds.
buildSteps.decision: IPs are stored only as HMAC hashes with a server salt.

buildSteps.title: Other backends
buildSteps.text: SQL through PDO, S3 and Google Cloud Storage behind the same interface.
buildSteps.decision: Backends implement one abstract class, so the rest of the server does not know where data lives.

buildSteps.title: Short links
buildSteps.text: An optional proxy to YOURLS, Shlink or Chhoto.
buildSteps.decision: The call goes through the server so the shortener's API key is not exposed in the browser.

tour.title: A pastebin the server cannot read
body: PrivateBin answers the classic pastebin question with a twist: the server stores only ciphertext.
People use it from a browser; the PHP server keeps encrypted blobs in a folder, a database or a bucket, and may call a URL shortener.
tour.why: The interview version stores text and serves it back. Here the hard part moves into the browser, and the server gets simpler.

tour.title: Encrypt before sending
body: Follow a new paste from the editor to the request body.
tour.why: Everything the server receives is already encrypted, so nothing on the server can leak the text.

tour.title: The server stores a blob
body: Rate limit, rules on the clear-text settings, and a write to storage.
tour.why: The server can enforce only what it can see: size, rate, expiry and burn after reading.

tour.title: The key stays in the fragment
body: The answer is an ID and a delete token; the browser adds the key after #.
tour.why: Whoever has the link has the key. That is the whole access model, so share links carefully.

tour.title: Reading: page, then data, then decrypt
body: The page is the same for every paste; the data comes as JSON and is decrypted in place.
tour.why: Expired and burned pastes are deleted on the server at the moment of reading.

tour.title: Cleanup without a cron job
body: Expired pastes are deleted in small batches while new ones are created.
tour.why: Nothing extra to deploy, at the cost of cleanup depending on traffic.

tour.title: The whole pastebin, on one map

recap.people: Authors write, readers open the link.
recap.browser: The browser makes the key and does all the crypto.
recap.server: One PHP entry point routes, limits and serves the page.
recap.outside: An optional shortener for long links.
recap.storage: Disk, SQL or a bucket, holding only ciphertext.
recap.rules: Expiry, burn after reading and cleanup on the server.

body: A JavaScript client that encrypts, a small PHP server and pluggable storage.
The design choice that shapes everything: the key never reaches the server.

crypto.title: Inside the browser crypto
crypto.sub: What CryptTool.cipher() does with a paste before it is sent. Decryption runs the same steps backwards.
crypto.cap: The settings that the server must read (format, discussion, burn after reading) are not encrypted but authenticated: they are part of the AES-GCM tag, so a changed flag makes decryption fail.

steps.d: 32 random bytes from the browser's crypto API; one key per paste.
A random IV and salt, 100,000 PBKDF2 rounds, AES-256-GCM, zlib unless the browser lacks WebAssembly.
The parameters and the clear-text options travel next to the ciphertext and are bound to it.
PBKDF2 over the random key and the password, if any.

steps.t: Put the key in the link
steps.d: base58 after #; with burn after reading, after #- so the reader confirms before the paste is fetched and deleted.

controller.title: Inside the controller: a new paste
controller.sub: What Controller::_create() does with a POST, in order. Early exits answer with a JSON error.
controller.cap: The same entry point handles comments: a body with a paste ID and a parent ID is a comment, stored next to its paste.

steps.d: POST means create; a paste ID with a delete token means delete; a paste ID alone means read.
Version, base64 fields, cipher parameters: the server validates the shape it cannot read.

exit.t: Stored under its paste and parent

steps.d: At most once every 5 minutes, up to 10 pastes.

steps.t: Answer with ID and delete token

paste.title: Inside the paste rules: reading
paste.sub: What Paste::get() does before a paste is handed out.
paste.cap: Expiry is checked when a paste is read, not only by the purge. An expired paste is never served, even if no cleanup has run for weeks.

exit.t: Does not exist, has expired or was deleted

steps.d: Delete it now and answer as if it never existed.
Deleted as it is returned: the first reader is the last.

sql.title: Inside the SQL database
sql.sub: Three tables, created on first use by Database.php. Hover a reference to see the table it points to.
sql.cap: There is no user table and no plaintext column: data is the whole encrypted JSON envelope. Only the expiry date is a separate column, so the purge can find old pastes without reading blobs.

fields.note: ciphertext, settings and attachments as JSON
creation time and the paste's salt
icon derived from the poster's IP hash

entries.t: The only PHP entry point: loads Composer's autoloader and builds the controller.
The whole PHP server, one class per file.
Picks the operation and answers with JSON or the page.
entries.why: All server behaviour starts here, so reading this one file shows every request type.

entries.t: Reads method, query string and JSON body into one operation.
Validates the shape of an encrypted envelope.
Paste and comment rules: expiry, burn after reading, IDs and delete tokens.
Builds the storage backend from the config and runs the purge.
Small server-side state: server salt, traffic limiter and purge limiter.
entries.why: These values live in the same store as the pastes, so a multi-server install shares them for free.

entries.t: One class per storage backend behind AbstractData.
entries.why: Adding a backend means one new class; nothing else changes.

entries.t: The whole client: UI, crypto and server calls in one file of modules.
entries.why: The security of the system rests on this file, since it is what handles keys and plaintext.

entries.t: zlib compiled to WebAssembly, used to compress before encrypting.
Every setting with its default: backend, limits, expiry options, shortener.
entries.why: Most behaviour on this map is switched here, so a real install may look different.

entries.t: Command line tool to purge, delete or list pastes and print statistics.
PHPUnit tests for the server; js/test holds the client tests.
entries.more: one test class per server class

entries.t: Hosting requirements and how to pick a backend.
